answer.label: Not Kurt Vonnegut — actually Robert Brault
answer.sourceLine: Kurt Vonnegut never wrote this. The line is the work of aphorist Robert Brault, who says he wrote it for the National Enquirer in 1985; Reader’s Digest reprinted it in its September 1986 issue. His original read “Enjoy the little things, for one day you may look back…” — the popular Vonnegut version adds “in life” and swaps in “you’ll.”

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: The Book of Positive Quotations (Fairview Press, 1997)

source.excerpt: Enjoy the little things, for one day you may look back and realize they were the big things.
trail: Robert Brault states plainly: “I wrote the quote for National Enquirer in 1985… reprinted by Reader’s Digest in its September 1986 issue” on his own site.
Brault notes that from 1986 to 2009 the line appeared in anthologies always credited to him, and that the Vonnegut misattribution only began around 2009.
The Vonnegut-credited wording is preserved on Goodreads, showing the reworded “in life…you’ll look back” variant.
source.excerptNote: Brault’s original wording. The version pinned on Vonnegut — “Enjoy the little things in life, for one day you’ll look back…” — is a lightly altered later variant.

source.rightsNote: The aphorism was written by a living author and first published in 1985 (National Enquirer; reprinted Reader’s Digest, 1986), so it is in copyright, with rights held by Robert Brault. The widely shared “Vonnegut” wording is a lightly altered variant of that copyrighted original, not a public-domain or independently sourced text.

author.name: Robert Brault
author.heading: About Robert Brault
author.bio: Robert Brault is an American freelance writer and aphorist, born in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1938, known for short, epigrammatic observations on everyday life. Many of his one-liners circulated for decades in anthologies and periodicals such as Reader’s Digest before the internet stripped his name from them. This aphorism — among his best known — is a textbook case: it drifted from a credited magazine filler into a viral “Vonnegut” meme.

misattribution.heading: How Vonnegut got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a clean case of a credited, copyrighted magazine aphorism being rebranded online under a famous novelist’s name.

items.why: No Vonnegut novel, essay, speech, or letter contains this line. The credit appears only on social media and quote sites; Brault documents that it surfaced around 2009, long after decades of correct attribution to him. See Brault’s account.
Brault’s original is “Enjoy the little things, for one day you may look back…” The viral form inserts “in life” and changes “may” to “you’ll,” as seen on the Vonnegut Goodreads page.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is aphorist Robert Brault, who published the line in 1985 — a decade before it was ever linked to Kurt Vonnegut.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Kurt Vonnegut is one of the internet’s great quote magnets: warm, plainspoken wisdom gets pinned to him because it sounds like something he’d say. But this gentle aphorism about savoring small moments has a paper trail that predates its Vonnegut phase by more than twenty years — and it points to a working aphorist, not a novelist.

Robert Brault made a living writing exactly these kinds of compact lines for magazines. When his name fell off the quote in the social-media era, a bigger name filled the vacuum — and the slightly smoothed wording (“in life…you’ll look back”) is itself a fingerprint of that unattributed re-sharing.
context.pull: A credited 1985 magazine line, rebranded as Vonnegut two decades later.
